extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (elementary/secondary schools, postsecondary institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, compliance officers, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for educational institutions and other recipients of federal funds to implement and comply with the Final Title IX regulations (duties of Title IX Coordinators, notification rules, supportive measures, grievance procedures, training, pregnancy/lactation accommodations, and scope of covered sex discrimination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator Obligations: Duty to Monitor (§106.44(b) and (f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX Coordinators must oversee a recipient's response to individual reports and required action to address and prevent future sex discrimination for all participants in a recipient's education program or activity; duties centralize responsibilities, promote accountability, and enable effective Title IX compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients have flexibility to determine which monitoring strategies fit their size and resources. Examples of low-cost monitoring include incorporating questions about barriers to reporting into existing trainings, roundtable discussions, listening sessions, and conversations with students/employees. Recipients may delegate specific duties to designees provided one Title IX Coordinator retains ultimate oversight (see §106.8(a)). Identifying patterns, trends, and risk factors and developing initiatives or trainings in response are part of monitoring. Costs of monitoring were assessed as de minimis in the Department's analysis unless commenters provided contrary data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification Requirements for Employees (§106.44(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees with notification duties must take action when they have information that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination under Title IX; requirements differ for elementary/secondary schools versus other recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary and secondary school recipients must require all non-confidential employees to notify the Title IX Coordinator when they have information that reasonably may constitute sex discrimination. For other recipients, two categories of non-confidential employees exist: (1) employees with authority to institute corrective measures or with responsibility for administrative leadership, teaching, or advising — must notify the Title IX Coordinator; (2) all other non-confidential employees — must either notify the Title IX Coordinator or provide the Title IX Coordinator's contact information and complaint process information. Recipients must train all employees on applicable notification requirements (§106.8(d)(1)(iii)), provide prompt training when employees change positions that alter Title IX duties, and annual retraining thereafter. Training and the act of notification are treated as de minimis costs in the Department's analysis. Recipients may simplify by training all non-confidential employees to notify the Title IX Coordinator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of Supportive Measures (§106.44(f)-(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are obligated to offer and provide supportive measures designed to restore or preserve a party's access to the recipient's education program or activity for all forms of sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must be 'reasonably available' and apply to the broader set of incidents covered by the final regulations. The Department expects an increase in the number of incidents in which supportive measures are offered (revised estimate raised from 1.5x to 2.0x the number of grievance-initiations); assumed 90% acceptance rate and estimated cost of $250 per incident. Recipients should consider coordination, implementation, and documentation of supportive measures; costs were analyzed and increased in the Regulatory Impact Analysis accordingly. Supportive measures are not limited to sexual harassment and are available across covered sex-discrimination incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial Review of Supportive Measures (§106.44(g)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide an appropriate, impartial employee to consider challenges to supportive measures decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a minimum, assigning one person to handle challenged decisions satisfies the requirement. This assignment imposes only negligible monetary cost per incident (de minimis cumulatively). The Department emphasizes the importance of independent review to ensure fairness and that this requirement does not compel creation of an extensive administrative structure; small institutions may rely on a single impartial employee distinct from the original decisionmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance Procedures Requirements (§§106.45 and 106.46)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must ensure fair, transparent, reliable outcomes for all sex discrimination complaints and include specific procedural safeguards and flexibility for recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required elements include notice of the allegations, an opportunity for parties to respond, an adequate, reliable, and impartial investigation, and an objective evaluation of all relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence. The final regulations apply one set of grievance procedures to all forms of sex discrimination, with additional procedures for sex-based harassment involving a postsecondary student party. Recipients retain significant discretion: reasonable timeframes, use of employees vs. contractors as investigators/decisionmakers, individual decisionmaker or panel, informal resolution options, choice of disciplinary sanctions, and appeal procedures. The final rules remove certain prescriptive 2020 requirements (e.g., mandatory live hearing, prohibition on single-investigator model, mandatory investigative report, specific written notice rules for K–12) while preserving fairness safeguards. The Department found that streamlining and clarity justify applying §§106.45/106.46 broadly and do not impose burdens that outweigh benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Stability and Reliance Interests
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department must weigh regulatory stability and reliance interests of recipients (e.g., prior incorporation of the 2020 amendments into policies, practices, collective bargaining agreements) when issuing changes to Title IX regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations retain and enhance many 2020 requirements or make provisions permissive (rather than mandatory) to mitigate disruption. The Department considered reliance interests and collective bargaining processes but concluded that the public benefits of the final regulations justify the changes; costs associated with renegotiating agreements were not estimated due to lack of data. Recipients should update policies and educate communities to promote understanding of rights and responsibilities under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training for Decisionmakers (§106.46(f)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisionmakers in the grievance process must receive training; the content will be adjusted to reflect the final regulations but training duration is not expected to increase materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients were already required to train decisionmakers under the 2020 amendments. The Department expects content changes rather than longer training; any administrative cost is justified by the benefits of equitable, transparent, and reliable grievance outcomes. For further details, see requirements and cost discussion in §106.8(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-Investigator Model Permitted (§106.45(b)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are permitted to use a single-investigator model in their grievance procedures as an option to resolve complaints of sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The single-investigator model can shorten timelines, leverage the investigator's knowledge to make determinations, increase scheduling efficiency, and may support quality grievance processes. The Department permits the model given reported benefits and to provide recipients flexibility; selection of this model remains within recipient discretion and is one of several permissible procedural designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Modifications for Pregnancy and Lactation Spaces (§§106.40 and 106.57(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must provide reasonable modifications to students who are pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions and must provide lactation spaces for students and employees that meet minimum standards for privacy, sanitation, and functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable modifications build on prior obligations and include adjustments like larger desks, more frequent bathroom breaks, temporary elevator access, or other individualized accommodations. The requirement applies to students who are pregnant or experiencing pregnancy-related conditions (not to partners or other family members). Lactation spaces need not be bathrooms, need not be dedicated 24/7 spaces, and need not meet a prescribed size — compliance can often be met using existing space with minimal cost (e.g., adding a chair or keypad lock). The Department does not require recipients to provide or pay for abortion-related services; notification and training costs associated with informing students of pregnancy rights are treated as de minimis and considered under Title IX Coordinator duties and training provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Sex Discrimination Coverage (§106.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations clarify the scope of sex discrimination covered by Title IX (including protections related to gender identity) and require recipients to apply Title IX protections broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying the scope may increase the number of complaints and associated costs for some recipients, but the Department found that the non-monetary benefits of clarity and fulfilling Title IX's broad protections justify implementation costs. Recipients should ensure policies and procedures encompass all individuals on the basis of sex, and the Department considered impacts across sexes while declining to limit protections. The final rule's scope changes were adopted despite commenters' concerns about administrative, financial, and legal costs.
